contract: construct() -> array of shape (N, 3) of nonzero vectors; each is normalised to the unit sphere. Score: the covering radius in degrees, max over points y of the sphere of the angular distance from y to the nearest configuration point (the largest circumradius of the facets of the convex hull, each facet checked to have an empty cap); minimize. Coincident points, configurations inside a closed hemisphere, numerically inconsistent hulls, a wrong shape or non-finite values make the candidate invalid.
notes: Independent implementation; the published record constructions (Packomania, the Hardin-Sloane-Smith covering table, the Amore-Figueroa-Ramos log-energy minima) were scored with this evaluator and reproduce the published values (validation/human-results/frontier_physics.json). No optimality is claimed for any value; a score beyond the record by more than the stated margin is a candidate new record that needs independent high-precision confirmation.
protocol_description: Locally implemented evaluator with recorded reference checks; consult the task-specific tests and evidence for their exact scope. This label alone does not establish reproduction of the paper's full experiment.
name: Covering the sphere with 130 equal caps
description: Place 130 points on the unit sphere so that the largest angular distance from any point of the sphere to its nearest chosen point (the covering radius) is as small as possible. The best known covering has radius 11.3153512 degrees: in 2026 Henry Cohn improved the 1994 value of Hardin, Sloane and Smith (11.3165625 degrees). It is not proven optimal.
benchmark: Covering the sphere with 130 equal caps
paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

sources.locator: Tarnai and Gáspár (1991), Covering a sphere by equal circles, and the rigidity of its graph: the covering problem, conjectured coverings for N = 15-20 and sporadic larger N.

Hardin, Sloane and Smith table of coverings by N spherical caps in 3 dimensions (calculations of 1994, maintained by H. Cohn; radii rounded up), row N = 130, read 2026-11-20: 11.3153512 degrees, credited to Henry Cohn, 2026 (the 1994 value was 11.3165625 degrees); coordinate files are named cov3-N.txt in the table's data set (whether its cov3-130.txt is the 2026 covering was not checked), and neilsloane.com/coverings/dim3/cover.3.130.txt is the 1994 covering.

limitations: The table gives covering radii rounded up to 1e-7 degrees; a covering counts as a new record only when it is below the table value by more than 1e-7 degrees. Optimal coverings are proven only for small N; the table value for N = 50 dates from 1994, and the value for N = 130 is Henry Cohn's 2026 improvement of the 1994 value.
Points are normalised to the unit sphere before scoring, so only directions matter; the record coordinates are public, so scores measure the returned construction, not the search that produced it.
Candidate Python runs inside the evaluator process and is trusted research code; the evaluator recomputes the score from the returned array but does not sandbox the program.

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find 130 points on the sphere whose equal caps of smallest possible angular radius cover the whole sphere.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Optimal spherical coverings bound the worst-case error of placing sites, sensors or quadrature points on the sphere; they are proven only for small N, and the records for larger N remain open to improvement: the 1994 record for N = 130 was improved in 2026.
